title: Recursion, base cases and recursive progress
learningObjectives: Identify the base case that terminates recursive calls.
Ensure each recursive step moves toward a base case.
Trace recursive calls and their return sequence.
Recognize stack/resource limits and arithmetic overflow risks.

understand.concept: A recursive function calls itself directly or indirectly. A correct recursive design has a base case and a recursive step that moves toward that base case. Each active call has its own automatic parameters and local objects. Recursion consumes execution resources, and mathematically correct logic can still overflow its C result type.
understand.whyItMatters: Recursion can express divide-and-conquer and naturally recursive structures, but missing or unreachable base cases can cause unbounded calls and stack exhaustion.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Recursive structure

A recursive function solves a problem by handling a simple base case and reducing other cases to a smaller instance of the same problem.

## 2. Base case

The base case stops further recursive calls. Without a reachable base case, recursion may continue until execution resources are exhausted.

## 3. Progress

Each recursive call must move closer to the base case. For a countdown, the argument should decrease and the base case should handle zero or another defined endpoint.

## 4. Trace the call stack

Each call has its own parameter and automatic local objects. Calls return in reverse order, so tracing both the call sequence and return sequence helps explain the result.

## 5. Resource and range limits

Deep recursion can exhaust stack resources. Integer arithmetic inside recursion can overflow. Define input limits and consider an iterative algorithm when it is simpler or safer.
